lesson_title: Gradient: One Formula, Four Lines, Full Marks
hook_text: 1:20 or 1:200 — one of these slopes breaks cyclists. Almost everyone picks the wrong one.
clip_script: The answer is written as a ratio in the form 1 to x, and the meaning of that form is wonderfully physical: for every 1 metre you rise, you move x metres across the ground. A gradient of 1 to 4 is punishing — a metre of climb for every four paces. A gradient of 1 to 400 spreads that same metre of climb across four hundred metres of walking — the ground feels flat. Which brings us to the interpretation rule that costs more marks than the arithmetic ever does: the bigger the number after the colon, the gentler the slope. The large number does not mean a large slope; it means your single metre of climbing has been thinned out over a longer walk.
visual_style: Split-screen cyclist grinding up a short sharp hill labelled 1:20 versus cruising a long shallow road labelled 1:200, ratio digits slamming onto screen as the comparison lands.
pacing: Rapid-fire hook, hard pause on the rule, snappy outro.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and lock in the four-line layout that banks every mark.
